name: Mycelial Immune Symbiont
description: Introduces a beneficial fungal symbiont — engineered from medicinal mushroom species — that colonizes the skin and mucosal membranes, creating a living biological shield. The mycelial network produces broad-spectrum antimicrobial compounds, accelerates wound healing at colonized sites, and provides an early-warning immune response by detecting pathogens before they penetrate the body. The symbiont is invisible to the naked eye but detectable as a faint earthy scent on the user's skin. In ideal conditions, the mycelium produces barely visible white filaments at wound sites that accelerate clotting and prevent infection — essentially a biological bandage that grows from the skin. Gravemoss Biofoundry engineered the symbiont from Trametes versicolor (turkey tail mushroom) and Ganoderma lucidum (reishi), both renowned for immune-modulating properties.
source_organism: Trametes versicolor (turkey tail mushroom), Ganoderma lucidum (reishi mushroom), engineered symbiotic strain
procedure: Topical application of symbiont starter culture with skin-integration medium, single session
expression_time: 2–4 weeks for initial colonization; full immune integration at 3 months
reversibility: Eliminable with antifungal treatment; immune benefits disappear within 2 weeks
side_effects: Faint earthy or mushroom scent on skin
Visible white mycelial filaments at wound sites (alarming to those unfamiliar)
Symbiont competes with normal skin flora — may cause temporary skin irritation during colonization
Antifungal medications kill the symbiont, requiring reinstallation
Rare: mycelial overgrowth in humid conditions producing visible fungal patches on skin
social_perception: Practical and mildly unusual. The earthy scent is distinctive but not unpleasant. The visible wound-healing filaments are unsettling until you understand what they are. In the Gray Zone, the modification is valued as affordable immune support. Some users cultivate the earthy aesthetic deliberately.
story_hooks: A Shroom Shield user's symbiont detects a pathogen in a sealed corporate building that the building's own sensors miss — the fungal network is more sensitive than electronic detection

A mycelial overgrowth event causes a user's skin to sprout visible mushroom fruiting bodies — alarming but harmless, and the spores carry the symbiont to nearby unmodified people, spreading the immune benefits without consent
